title: Stock Price Fluctuation
description:
# Stock Price Fluctuation

You receive a stream of updates for one stock. Each update gives a `timestamp` and the stock `price` at that timestamp.

Updates may arrive out of chronological order, and an update may correct the price for a timestamp that was already recorded. Only the newest price for each timestamp is active.

Design a data structure that supports:

*   Recording or correcting the price at a timestamp.
*   Returning the price at the latest timestamp currently recorded.
*   Returning the maximum active price across all timestamps.
*   Returning the minimum active price across all timestamps.

Implement the `StockPrice` class:

*   `StockPrice()` initializes the object with no price records.
*   `void update(int timestamp, int price)` records or corrects the price at `timestamp`.
*   `int current()` returns the price at the largest timestamp seen so far.
*   `int maximum()` returns the largest active price.
*   `int minimum()` returns the smallest active price.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input:**
["StockPrice", "update", "update", "current", "maximum", "update", "maximum", "update", "minimum"]
[[], [1, 10], [2, 5], [], [], [1, 3], [], [4, 2], []]
**Output:**
[null, null, null, 5, 10, null, 5, null, 2]
**Explanation:**
StockPrice stockPrice = new StockPrice();
stockPrice.update(1, 10); // active prices: {1 -> 10}
stockPrice.update(2, 5);  // active prices: {1 -> 10, 2 -> 5}
stockPrice.current();     // returns 5 because timestamp 2 is latest
stockPrice.maximum();     // returns 10
stockPrice.update(1, 3);  // correct timestamp 1 from 10 to 3
stockPrice.maximum();     // returns 5 because timestamp 1 no longer has price 10
stockPrice.update(4, 2);  // active prices: {1 -> 3, 2 -> 5, 4 -> 2}
stockPrice.minimum();     // returns 2

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= timestamp, price <= 10^9`
*   At most `3 * 10^4` calls will be made to `update`, `current`, `maximum`, and `minimum`.
*   `current`, `maximum`, and `minimum` will be called only after `update` has been called at least once.

solutions.name: HashMap with TreeMap Price Counts
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per update, O(1) for current/maximum/minimum
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store the active price for each timestamp in a `HashMap`. Store active price frequencies in a `TreeMap`, and track the largest timestamp seen so far.

## Key Insight

When an old timestamp is corrected, its previous price must be removed from the active multiset before the new price is inserted. Frequency counts make duplicate prices safe.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: `update` costs O(log n); `current`, `maximum`, and `minimum` cost O(1).
- Space Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of active timestamps.

solutions.name: Dual Heaps with Lazy Deletion
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep the active timestamp-to-price map. Push every update into both a max-heap and a min-heap as `(price, timestamp)`, and clean stale heap entries only when answering extrema queries.

## Key Insight

Java priority queues cannot delete arbitrary old entries cheaply. The active map acts as a version check, so stale heap entries can be discarded when they reach the top.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: `update` costs O(log q). Each stale heap entry is removed once, so `maximum` and `minimum` are amortized O(log q).
- Space Complexity: O(q), where q is the number of updates stored in the heaps.

solutions.name: Ordered Active Records TreeSet
solutions.timeComplexity: O(log n) per update, O(1) for current/maximum/minimum
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent each active timestamp as a record. Store the current record in a map by timestamp, and store all active records in a `TreeSet` ordered by price and timestamp.

## Key Insight

The ordered set contains only active records. Correcting a timestamp means removing exactly its old record before adding the replacement record.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: `update` costs O(log n); `current`, `maximum`, and `minimum` cost O(1).
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree over Price Values
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store active timestamp prices in a map. Maintain active price frequencies in a dynamic segment tree over the value range `[1, 10^9]`, where each node stores how many active prices lie in its range.

## Key Insight

The price domain is huge but sparse. A dynamic tree creates only paths touched by updates, while still supporting min and max by walking toward the first non-empty child.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: O(log V) for updates and extrema queries, where V is the price value range.
- Space Complexity: O(k log V) nodes in the worst case for k distinct prices touched by updates.

solutions.name: HashMap Counts with On-Demand Extremum Rebuild
solutions.timeComplexity: O(1) average update unless an invalidated extremum requires O(d) rebuild
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use hash maps for timestamp prices and price frequencies. Track the current minimum and maximum prices directly, and rebuild those two values by scanning distinct active prices only when the removed old price was the last copy of an extremum.

## Key Insight

This baseline avoids ordered containers. It is still correct because every query reads cached extrema that are repaired immediately when a correction invalidates them.

## Complexity Analysis

- Time Complexity: average O(1) update when extrema stay valid; O(d) rebuild when the last current minimum or maximum is removed, where d is the number of distinct active prices. Queries are O(1).
- Space Complexity: O(n + d).
